newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels say sick hostages will not be freed.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels say sick hostages will not be freed.

text.p: Peruvian rebels holding 72 VIPs for 65 days said on Thursday no more hostages would be freed on medical grounds, claiming their captives could get adequate treatment inside the besieged Japanese ambassador's home.

The 20-odd heavily armed rebels holed up in the residence "will not allow the evacuation of any more (hostages). Their treatment is possible inside the residence," the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) said in a statement.
Despite more sophisticated medical attention in the last few weeks, concern for the hostages' health has grown as they show increasing signs of stress after 65 days in captivity.

Enriqueta de Mendoza appealed to Nestor Cerpa Cartolini, the rebel leader inside the residence, to release her husband, Energy and Mines Vice Minister Juan Mendoza, who has a hernia. "He has the medical report. I do not know what Mr. Cerpa is waiting for," she told reporters outside the residence.

Other hostages required close monitoring for cancer, heart problems and arthritis and the government and doctors visiting the hostages, mainly middle-aged men, have warned there may be health emergencies. The last two hostages released from the compound were freed on medical grounds.

But the MRTA refused to take direct responsibility for their hostages' deteriorating health. "Any illness is the product of negotiations dragging on," said the statement issued over the Internet on behalf of the MRTA's high command.

The government and rebels have not set a date for new talks but there were signs the MRTA could roll back its demands, allowing progress toward a peaceful solution. In an interview with Reuters at a secret jungle location this week the group said publicly for the first time it probably would not win its central demand that all jailed comrades be freed.

"I do not think all of the 400-plus are going to get out," said a man who identified himself as "Comrade Alejandro," a member of the MRTA's top policy-making body. He said the MRTA was prepared to negotiate how many comrades should be released depending on their experience and importance in the movement.
But the jungle commander said he doubted Cerpa would ever drop completely the demand for the release of jailed rebels.

The hostage-takers in Lima have repeatedly said they will never give up their main demand, but the start of face-to-face talks with the government last week raised speculation they might shift their position.
The Argentine human rights group Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo said on Wednesday it had accepted an offer from the rebels to mediate in talks over the fate of the 72 hostages.

But MRTA international spokesman Isaac Velazco told Reuters: "I am sure that the government would not accept the mediation of a human rights group." He added that he made a general call to human rights groups that "they contribute to bringing about a peaceful solution".

Hebe de Bonafini, president of the group formed during the Argentine military's "Dirty War" against leftist guerrillas in the 1970s, said she would be in Lima on Friday and hoped to meet President Alberto Fujimori and see MRTA prisoners.
Vatican, Red Cross and Canadian government representatives are serving on a commission of guarantors, set up under an agreement by both sides, to keep the talks going.
